title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Three: Message Header Extensions for Non-ASCII Text
summary: The third MIME document. It extends the older email message format to let non-ASCII text appear in header fields, such as names and subjects, using an encoding that older systems can still carry.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME Part Three defines a way to put non-ASCII characters (like accented letters or non-Latin scripts) in email headers. It uses an encoded form that old systems still read as ASCII text.

subtitle: Encoding non-ASCII text in email headers without breaking existing mail systems

tldr.problem: Email headers (like Subject) were historically limited to ASCII; adding non-ASCII characters directly broke older systems.
tldr.mechanism: Defines the encoded-word syntax: =?charset?encoding?text?= where encoding is B (base64) or Q (quoted-printable), allowing non-ASCII text in headers.
tldr.outcome: Enabled internationalized email headers while remaining compatible with existing ASCII-based mail systems; updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: Certain header fields only (not message body)

today: RFC 2047 is a Draft Standard and has not been obsoleted; it was updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231. Its encoded-word syntax remains widely used in email headers for internationalized text.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 2047 defines encoded-words as a mechanism for embedding non-ASCII text in certain portions of RFC 822/MIME message headers. It was published as part of MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) to allow internationalized text in fields like Subject, To, From, and Sender without breaking existing mail software.

The RFC specifies that encoded-words must only be used where the character set of the header cannot directly represent the text. It also defines the syntax =?charset?encoding?text?=, where charset names a character set (e.g., ISO-8859-1), encoding is B for base64 or Q for a modified quoted-printable form, and text is the encoded data.
sections.plainLanguage: Email headers used to only accept English letters and symbols. RFC 2047 lets you include other characters (like é or 汉字) by wrapping them in a special encoded form that old email programs still treat as plain text.

sections.title: Encoded-Word Syntax
sections.content:
The encoded-word is: =? <charset> ? <encoding> ? <encoded-text> ?=. All components are ASCII. The charset is an IANA-registered character set name. The encoding is either B (base64) or Q (similar to quoted-printable, but space becomes underscore and certain characters are represented differently).

The Q encoding is designed for readability in headers: spaces may be represented as _ (underscore), and printable ASCII characters that are not special in this syntax can remain as-is (except ?, =, and _ which must be encoded). The B encoding uses base64 and is more compact for many non-Latin scripts.

Encoded-words are atomic; white space and other text should not be inserted inside them. Also, encoded-words MUST NOT be used in certain contexts where they would be ambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: The encoded form looks like =?UTF-8?B?...?=. It tells the email program what character set to use and whether the data was scrambled by base64 (B) or a header-friendly quoted form (Q). This keeps everything readable as ASCII on the wire.

sections.title: When and How to Use Encoded-Words
sections.content:
Encoded-words may appear in header fields that contain unstructured text (like Subject) or in structured fields in places where text values occur, as long as they are used to represent characters not directly representable in ASCII. They must not be used to encode purely ASCII text that could be represented directly.

Multiple encoded-words can be concatenated (optionally separated by linear white space) to represent a longer string; the whitespace between adjacent encoded-words is ignored by decoders. This allows breaking long encoded strings across lines while remaining valid.

Encoded-words are not intended for use in the body of messages; that is the domain of MIME content transfer encodings defined in other parts of MIME. They are specifically for header fields as defined in RFC 2047.

Encoded-words MUST NOT be nested. If you need multiple character sets in one logical unit, the RFC specifies the constraints; generally, each encoded-word represents text in one charset.
sections.plainLanguage: Only use encoded-words when you need non-ASCII characters in a header. You can string several together if the text is long, but don't nest them. And don't use this trick in the message body - that's handled differently.

sections.title: Practical Notes
sections.content:
The RFC requires that mail software be able to both encode and decode encoded-words. When encoding, implementations should choose a suitable charset and prefer B or Q encoding based on efficiency. When decoding, unknown charsets should be treated with care (typically as per MIME charset handling).

Encoded-words are case-insensitive for the charset and encoding tokens. However, the encoded text is case-sensitive depending on the character set and encoding. The maximum length considerations follow from header line length limits in RFC 822.

RFC 2047 obsoleted earlier work in RFC 1521, RFC 1522, and RFC 1590. It was later updated by RFC 2184 (which clarified content-disposition and other aspects related to MIME parameters) and RFC 2231 (which extended parameter encoding beyond encoded-words in a related form).
sections.plainLanguage: Email programs need to be able to read and write these encoded headers. The encoded-words follow specific rules so they work with older systems, and the design has been refined in later RFCs to handle more complex cases.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that encoded-words can be used to obscure text. However, this is not a security feature - it is an encoding for compatibility. Mail clients must decode them to display meaningful text.

There are no strong cryptographic guarantees; the encoding provides no confidentiality or authentication. The main security consideration is that decoders must properly handle malformed encoded-words to avoid buffer overflows or other parsing issues (a common concern in older implementations).
sections.plainLanguage: The encoding just makes text displayable; it doesn't hide or protect it. As with any text parsing, programs must be careful not to crash on badly formed encoded-words.
